A quine is a program that takes no input and prints its own source code as its only output.
The idea matters because it turns self-reference into something executable: the program is both the description and the thing being described.

Quines are usually treated as exploratory or recreational programs rather than production techniques, but they are a sharp way to think about self-reference, interpretation, and fixed points in programming languages.
The term is associated with Person/Douglas Hofstadter/Book/79/Gödel, Escher, Bach and the broader tradition of indirect self-reference.
A proper quine does not read its own source file, fetch hidden input, or otherwise "cheat" by relying on the surrounding filesystem.
The usual trick is to separate the program into printing logic and a textual representation of the whole program, then arrange for each part to emit the other.
Languages with strong quoting, reflection, or eval facilities can make quines shorter, but the underlying idea is still self-description plus re-emission.
Most quines keep a string or data structure that contains a printable representation of their own body.
The runtime prints the surrounding scaffolding, then a quoted or escaped form of that representation, then the remainder of the program.
In that sense, a quine is a fixed point of the execution environment: running it preserves the program text instead of transforming it into some unrelated result.
Quines are common programming puzzles in languages like Lisp, Python, Ruby, JavaScript, C, and shell, with the exact construction shaped by each language's quoting rules.
They are also a useful bridge between playful code-golf culture and deeper results such as recursion theorems and self-referential constructions.
A program that simply copies its file from disk is related, but it is not usually considered a proper quine.
A quine does not need to be practically useful in product code to be conceptually useful; its value is mostly explanatory rather than operational.

Quick reference guide to the RCA (phono) connector family
One RCA connector carries one signal; stereo audio needs a pair, component video needs three
Same physical connector shape is reused across several signal types, distinguished mainly by color coding
White or black: left channel analog audio
Green / Blue / Red trio: component video (Y/Pb/Pr)
Introduced by the Radio Corporation of America (RCA) in the late 1930s/1940s to connect phonograph players to radio receivers, hence "phono connector"
Became the de facto standard for consumer analog audio/video well before any formal single specification existed

Female RCA jack (socket), the receptacle mounted on a device that receives a male RCA plug
Coaxial design: a center pin receptacle carries the signal, surrounded by a barrel that grounds against the plug's outer shell
Almost always panel-mounted — on the back or side of audio/video equipment, rarely found on the end of a cable
Carries a single signal per jack; devices expose one jack per channel/signal (e.g. a stereo pair, or a video + audio trio)
Barrel inner diameter: sized to accept the ~9.5 mm male shell

Green / Blue / Red trio: component video (Y/Pb/Pr)

No single formal specification; the connector is a de facto standard maintained through consumer-electronics manufacturer compatibility

Official CLI: There is currently no official Readwise CLI tool. However, open-source alternatives exist for command-line interaction with Readwise Reader.
Tools to Connect AI Agents with Readwise Reader & Highlights

Readwise Reader CLI (rw-cli) – An open-source Python CLI by Scarvy that interacts with the Readwise Reader API. It supports adding new items (documents) to your Reader library and listing documents with various filters . For example, you can use rw-cli add <URL> to save an article, or rw-cli list --location later --category article to list saved articles (with options to filter by location like new, later, archive, or by category and date)

Official MCP Server: Readwise provides an official MCP server (@readwise/readwise-mcp on NPM) which is maintained by the Readwise team. This server allows AI clients (like Claude or Cursor) to search and retrieve highlights from your Readwise account . It focuses on the main Readwise highlights (e.g. Kindle/book highlights) rather than full Reader documents, and is regularly updated (v0.0.7 as of late 2025).

Readwise Reader MCP (edricgsh) – A popular open-source TypeScript MCP server that exposes the entire Readwise Reader API to AI agents . It gives your AI full control over your Reader library, supporting full CRUD on documents (create/save new articles, list/filter documents, update metadata like tags/folder, and delete documents) as well as tag listing and powerful regex search across content . This server is built with the official Claude SDK and is actively maintained; it had ~3.6k downloads by Oct 2025 , indicating healthy usage.
